questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the basic principles of ethics?

options.text: Autonomy
Justice
Paternalism
Nonmaleficence
Beneficence

correct_answer.text: Paternalism

correct_answers.text: Paternalism

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C Autonomy, justice, beneficence, and nonmaleficence are the four basic ethical principles.

questions.question_text: A patient was admitted to a psychiatric unit for suicidal ideation. Before initiating treatment, the treating psychiatrist explains the treatment procedure and obtains the patient’s consent to start medication after discussing alternative treatments, risks, and benefits. Which ethical principle did the psychiatrist follow in doing the above?

options.text: Justice
Autonomy
Beneficence
Paternalism
Competence

correct_answer.text: Autonomy

correct_answers.text: Autonomy

questions.explanation: ANSWER: B Asking the patient to consent to treatment is an example of respecting a patient's autonomy. The physician must obtain patient's informed consent for tests and treatment. The physician should disclose information that the average person would need to know to make an informed medical decision. This information should include benefits, risks, costs, and alternatives to the proposed treatment. If the patient lacks medical capacity, the physician must obtain informed consent from an appropriate surrogate. Of note, a health care proxy is a document that allows a person to appoint another person (the agent of that proxy) to act as a surrogate for medical decisions. Strictly speaking, the word proxy should not be used to describe the surrogate for medical decisions.

questions.question_text: “First do no harm” refers to which of the basic ethical principles?

options.text: Beneficence
Autonomy
Justice
Nonmaleficence
Fiduciary duty

correct_answer.text: Nonmaleficence

correct_answers.text: Nonmaleficence

questions.explanation: ANSWER: D Nonmaleficence is the duty to do no harm. Beneficence is the principle under which physicians help patients and relieve suffering. Autonomy is the principle that a patient has a right to control what happens to his or her own body and make decisions freely and without coercion. Justice is fairness to equal resources/access to care. Fiduciary duty is the principle to work in the patient's best interests.

questions.question_text: A 14- year- old boy is brought by his mother to a neurologist in your group practice. The mother requests that the boy be tested for the Huntingtin gene because the boy’s father was recently diagnosed with Huntington’s disease. What should be the most appropriate response of the neurologist?

options.text: Do the testing as per the mother’s request.
Require consent from both parents.
Do the testing only if the boy consents.
Inform the mother to bring the patient after 18 years.
Explain why this test is not appropriate to be performed at this time.

correct_answer.text: Explain why this test is not appropriate to be performed at this time.

correct_answers.text: Explain why this test is not appropriate to be performed at this time.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: E Presymptomatic testing for Huntington's disease should be performed only voluntarily at the request of an at-risk patient. It should not be ordered by others, and ordering should not be coerced by others. Such testing should not be ordered in minors who cannot give valid consent. Predictive testing should not be offered to minors or used in cases in which it would determine the carrier state of a relative who did not wish to know. It has also been argued that insurance companies and others with a financial interest should be precluded by law from asking for information on carrier state. Skilled counseling would be essential.

questions.question_text: A patient calls your office 1 hour prior to her actual appointment and informs you that she will not be able to attend that day’s session because an emergency came up at work. What would you do in regard to charging the patient for the missed session?

options.text: Do not charge because she called before her appointment time.
Charge for the session if this is a self- pay patient.
Charge the patient for not calling well in advance.
Cancel all future appointments.
The decision to charge depends on advance agreement.

correct_answer.text: The decision to charge depends on advance agreement.

correct_answers.text: The decision to charge depends on advance agreement.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: E Patients need to be informed about a doctor's policies for missed appointments during initial visits. The individual physician determines treatment policies, but patients must know in advance to be able to make an informed decision about whether to accept the doctor's policy or to choose another doctor.

questions.question_text: What are the ethical guidelines in regard to accepting gifts from patients?

options.text: Psychiatrists should accept any gift given by a patient to prevent the patient from feeling rejected.
Psychiatrists should never accept a gift from a patient.
Any gift worth less than $500 can readily be accepted.
Accepting a small gift from a patient is acceptable under certain circumstances.
None of the above.

correct_answer.text: Accepting a small gift from a patient is acceptable under certain circumstances.

correct_answers.text: Accepting a small gift from a patient is acceptable under certain circumstances.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: D The details of the case are important in determining whether or not to accept the gift. Exploitation involves using the therapeutic relationship for personal gain, such as hiring a patient or going into business with a patient. A physician should not have any business interactions with patient aside from payment for treatment.

questions.question_text: A patient can be involuntarily hospitalized under which of the following circumstances?

options.text: A patient poses imminent danger to him- or herself.
A patient poses imminent danger to others.
A patient demonstrates inability to meet basic needs.
All of the above.

correct_answer.text: All of the above.

correct_answers.text: All of the above.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: D Involuntary hospitalization is usually justified by a patient's imminent danger to him or herself or others, or an inability to meet basic needs. To meet these criteria, danger must be likely in the near future and related to a major mental illness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT required of a psychiatrist to avoid patient abandonment?

options.text: Give the patient enough time to find a new therapist.
Help the patient find a new therapist.
Provide a letter of termination.
Provide medical records requested by the new therapist.
Provide enough medication to last beyond the date of termination.

correct_answer.text: Provide enough medication to last beyond the date of termination.

correct_answers.text: Provide enough medication to last beyond the date of termination.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: E It is unethical for a psychiatrist to terminate a patient without providing a proper referral. It is not unethical to refrain from providing medication beyond the termination date.

questions.question_text: Psychiatrists have an ethical obligation to do all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Report physician impairment
Participate in executions
Report physician incompetence
Report ethical misconduct
Report child abuse

correct_answer.text: Participate in executions

correct_answers.text: Participate in executions

questions.explanation: ANSWER: B Psychiatrists should not participate in torture, interrogations, or executions. Psychiatrists have the ethical obligation to report physician impairment, incompetence, and ethical misconduct, as well as to report child (and elder) abuse.

questions.question_text: For how long should a patient’s medical records be kept by a psychiatrist?

options.text: Only as long as the patient is in treatment
Until billing is submitted to the patient’s insurance company
As long as possible
Indefinitely
Not consistently defined by statutes

correct_answer.text: Not consistently defined by statutes

correct_answers.text: Not consistently defined by statutes

questions.explanation: ANSWER: E There is no clear answer. Due to the variety of statutes, regulations, legal principles, and professional obligations affecting psychiatric records, the best risk management advice dictates that records should be kept for as long as possible. The safest and most conservative option is to never destroy patient records (i.e., keep records indefinitely). Perpetual maintenance may seem excessive, but there are many reasons the records may be needed in the future. If records cannot be kept indefinitely, they should be for as long.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is considered unethical behavior for a psychiatrist?

options.text: Transferring the care of a patient after noting romantic feelings toward the patient
Avoiding romantic relationships with a patient or ex- patient
Treating a new patient with whom the psychiatrist was sexually involved several years ago
Seeking supervision for erotic countertransference

correct_answer.text: Treating a new patient with whom the psychiatrist was sexually involved several years ago

correct_answers.text: Treating a new patient with whom the psychiatrist was sexually involved several years ago

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C Sexual activity with current and former patients is unethical. Likewise, any occasion in which the physician interacts with a current or former patient in ways that may preclude an intimate and nonprofessional relationship (as a date, intimate friend, etc.) should be avoided. Sex with patients or former patients is not acceptable under any circumstances. No former sexual partners should be accepted as patients.

questions.question_text: A 22- year- old patient recently diagnosed with schizophrenia presents with symptoms of paranoid delusions. He declines medication when he is alone with you but accepts in the presence of his mother, of whom he is paranoid. How should treatment proceed?

options.text: Do not start the medication because the patient’s decision is influenced by the presence of his mother.
Start the medication because the patient has provided consent.
Await consent from the father.
Offer the patient a long- acting injectable medication.
Give the medication only when the mother is present.

correct_answer.text: Do not start the medication because the patient’s decision is influenced by the presence of his mother.

correct_answers.text: Do not start the medication because the patient’s decision is influenced by the presence of his mother.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: A This is a difficult clinical situation, and this question highlights the importance of respecting a patient's autonomy. Autonomy is the principle that a patient has a right to control what happens to his or her own body and make decisions freely and without coercion. Ethically speaking, if a patient cannot provide informed consent for medication, then pursuing surrogate consent from the local probate court (depending on local statute) would be appropriate.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist performing a psychiatric evaluation to determine suitability for employment must inform the patient that:

options.text: The patient’s employer has the right to withhold examination results from the patient.
The patient should be truthful.
There are limits to the patient’s confidentiality.
The employer and the psychiatrist determine what information will be released.
The patient must comply with the treatment recommendations if treatment is indicated.

correct_answer.text: There are limits to the patient’s confidentiality.

correct_answers.text: There are limits to the patient’s confidentiality.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C Patients should be informed of the limits of confidentiality at the beginning of the physician-patient relationship and as events arise that create potential revelations.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an acceptable boundary crossing by a psychiatrist?

options.text: Meeting a patient over dinner for a session
Accepting an expensive wristwatch as a Christmas gift from a patient
Visiting a patient with a severe physical illness at home
Telling the patient explicit details about the psychiatrist’s romantic relationship

correct_answer.text: Visiting a patient with a severe physical illness at home

correct_answers.text: Visiting a patient with a severe physical illness at home

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C Boundary violations are transgressions that are immediately harmful, are likely to cause future harm, or are exploitive of the patient. Boundary crossings are deviations from customary behavior, but they do not necessarily harm the patient and may allow for flexibility within the therapy.

questions.question_text: If a patient’s spouse emails the psychiatrist with questions regarding the patient’s treatment, how should the psychiatrist proceed?

options.text: Reply to the email and answer the spouse’s questions.
Call the patient to request verbal permission to communicate with the spouse.
Do not reply to the email.
Call the spouse to explain that email communication is not permitted.

correct_answer.text: Do not reply to the email.

correct_answers.text: Do not reply to the email.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C In practices in which email is used as a means of communication, patients should sign a written agreement for communication via email and should be provided with a written policy during the initial visit. Guidelines include that email should not be for emergent or serious issues, and staff will not respond to emails from family members or others.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist refers patients to a drug abuse treatment facility, and she accepts $100 from the facility for each referral. Under which law can she be prosecuted?

options.text: Anti- Kickback Statute
False Claims Act
Stark Law
HIPAA
None of the above

correct_answer.text: Anti- Kickback Statute

correct_answers.text: Anti- Kickback Statute

questions.explanation: ANSWER: A The Anti-Kickback Statute prohibits the knowing, willful solicitation, receipt, or remuneration for patient referral or acquisition of goods or services for which payment is made under Medicare/Medicaid. A false claim is a claim submitted for reimbursement that misrepresents the type, price, description, or medical reason that necessitated the expense. The Stark Law prohibits physician self-referral. HIPAA is the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 that protects health information.

questions.question_text: An example of a false claim is:

options.text: A service that is billed but never provided
A diagnostic code used that does not match the diagnosis of the client
Upcoding or billing for a higher level of service than what was provided
Billing for unreasonable or unnecessary services
All of the above

correct_answer.text: All of the above

correct_answers.text: All of the above

questions.explanation: ANSWER: E A false claim is a claim submitted for reimbursement that misrepresents the type, price, description, or medical reason that necessitated the expense.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT one of the four basic elements that must be proved by the patient (or a surrogate on behalf of the patient) in order for the plaintiff to prevail in cases of malpractice?

options.text: Duty of care to the patient
Breach of duty
Damages caused by breach of duty
Deviation from standard of care
Injury caused directly by breach of duty

correct_answer.text: Deviation from standard of care

correct_answers.text: Deviation from standard of care

questions.explanation: ANSWER: D The injured patient must show that the physician acted negligently in rendering care and that such negligence resulted in injury. To do so, four legal elements must be proved: a professional duty owed to the patient; breach of such duty; injury caused by the breach; and resulting damages. In terms of the '4 Ds,' dereliction of duty directly causes damages. Physicians often deviate from standard of care per patient preference and may do so in a variety of instances where there are countervailing clinical and medical considerations at play.

questions.question_text: What are the current guidelines to publish scientific papers on patient cases in psychiatry?

options.text: A treating psychiatrist can publish case reports for scientific advancement.
Psychiatrists are prohibited from publishing any case reports of active patients or ex- patients.
Case reports can be published only after removing identifying patient information.
Scientific papers can be published after receiving verbal approval from patients.
A written informed consent is mandatory to publish case reports in psychiatry.

correct_answer.text: Case reports can be published only after removing identifying patient information.

correct_answers.text: Case reports can be published only after removing identifying patient information.

questions.explanation: ANSWER: C Informed consent from the patient is not required to publish case reports, but all identifying information should be hidden to protect the patient's confidentiality.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT true about informed consent?

options.text: There are exceptions to informed consent.
Information can be withheld by the doctor in special circumstances if it is damaging to the patient.
Patients may waive the right to informed consent.
All medical situations, even emergencies, require informed consent.
Parents should provide informed consent for children.

correct_answer.text: All medical situations, even emergencies, require informed consent.

correct_answers.text: All medical situations, even emergencies, require informed consent.

questions.explanation: ANSWER D The following are the important exceptions to informed consent: 1. Genuine emergencies do not require informed consent. Emergency care occurs in the framework of implied or presumed consent. That is, in emergency situations in which reasonable persons would want the intervention, it is ethical to proceed as if consent exists. 2. Care for children or incompetent patients requires consent from parents or legally recognized surrogates. Assent of incompetent individuals (i.e., acquiescence as opposed to informed consent) is obtained whenever possible. 3. Patients may waive their right to informed consent. This exception, however, presumes competence to do so. 4. The doctrine of therapeutic privilege allows a physician to withhold information if it is truly damaging to the patient, but such exceptions are rare. Withholding information about side-effects of medications in the hope of improving adherence is unacceptable.
